articles.title: MCP, MHS and the End of the Automation Pyramid?
articles.description:
Is the traditional automation pyramid becoming obsolete? And what happens when AI agents can directly interact with industrial machines, laboratory equipment and production systems?

In this episode of the Industrial AI Podcast, host Peter Seeberg welcomes Jan Wokittel, Director Smart Manufacturing at Roche, to explore how artificial intelligence, open standards and new protocols could fundamentally reshape industrial automation.

At the center of the discussion are Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Model Hardware Standard (MHS), two emerging approaches that could enable AI agents to move beyond analyzing data and generating code toward interacting with physical equipment.

Jan shares insights into Roche's experience with emerging AI technologies, including discussions and the potential implications for established automation ecosystems built around OPC UA, MQTT and traditional industrial software.

In this episode:

The end of the automation pyramid? Why traditional hierarchical architectures may no longer meet the demands of modern manufacturing.

MCP and MHS: How new interfaces could connect AI agents with industrial hardware.

AI provider versus traditional automation: Why AI companies could challenge established players such as Siemens and ABB.

Closing the loop: How AI agents could move from data analysis to executing actions in the physical world.

The future of industrial software: Why AI-powered development and open-source technologies could dramatically reduce software costs.

From concept to factory: How Jan used AI agents to design a virtual chocolate production line over a weekend.

Safety and validation: Why regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing presents particular challenges for autonomous AI systems.

One of the most provocative questions of the conversation: What happens to the value of industrial software when AI makes developing it dramatically faster and cheaper?

A conversation about the future of manufacturing, the growing influence of AI companies on industrial automation, and why machine builders may need to rethink their technology strategies.

Guest: Jan Wokittel, Director Smart Manufacturing, Roche

Host: Peter Seeberg, Industrial AI Podcast

Presented by NXAI — Your partner for time-series foundation models and Physical AI.

Weighing a Feather: How to Design A/B Tests That Work (Ep. 1046 with Billur Engin)
articles.description:
In Episode #1046, Billur Engin (who leads data science and analytics at Prolific) joins  ⁨@JonKrohnLearns to explain how to design experiments that actually teach you something. Too many A/B tests, she says, are like bathroom scales trying to weigh a feather — the effect is real, but the system was never built to detect it. In her first-ever podcast appearance, Billur walks through why complexity has to earn its place in your models, the biggest myth about A/B testing, the AA test she runs to catch broken measurement, three ways to get at causality when you can’t run a controlled experiment, and why causal inference matters more than ever now that prediction has become cheap.

In this episode you will learn:
• (00:00) Introduction
• (01:18) What Prolific does and why representative data matters
• (05:19) Why complexity has to earn its place
• (07:29) The biggest myth about A/B testing
• (11:34) Why causal inference matters more than ever
• (14:39) Getting at causality when you can’t run an experiment

Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1046

articles.title: SPS 26: Beyond Components: AI and electrical topologies
articles.description:
In this episode, I talk to Dr. Fabian Distel and Dr. Julian Feinauer (Murrelektronik)about using AI to rethink how machines are designed, installed, and maintained. Their U-Konn-X Creaited uses specialized machine-learning models and engineering rules to generate and validate electrical topologies, while keeping the system open to components from different vendors.

We also get into why an LLM isn’t the right tool for every industrial problem, how agents could make these systems easier to use, and what it takes to turn digital tools into a business. The bigger question: can AI help manufacturers improve the whole system—not just shave a little cost off one component?
